text:
Discussing Solutions and Strategies

The goal of this problem is for students to see the relationship that the circumference is a little more than 3 times the diameter for any circle. The discussion of their work should come back to this core idea for each item discussed. (Language)

Suggested Questions

  • What do you notice about the data in the class graph? (Answers will vary. Emphasize that the data has a linear trend. Emphasize that a pattern exists between the diameter and the circumference lengths.)
  • What does this pattern suggest? (Answers will vary.)

This is a conversation from one classroom as they looked at their class data.

Teacher: I noticed that as you discussed your findings as a small group, some of us weren’t sure about a relationship between the diameter and circumference of the circular objects we had in our room. Does this class graph tell us anything?

Greg: When all of our dots got put together on this graph, it looks like it is almost a line.

Aponi: It does! I thought our group’s data might be a line, but one of our dots seemed too far off. But when I see the whole class data, I’m thinking maybe we didn’t measure as accurately as we should have.

(Many students begin nodding.)

Chase: Isn’t that like when we did the dripping faucet experiment in Moving Straight Ahead? Our data then wasn’t a perfect line because we weren’t super accurate, but it was close, and we could use it to make predictions.

Teacher: So what does this graph tell us about the relationship between the diameter and circumference of a circular object?

Aponi: Well, basically it is a linear relationship

Alyana: So if it is linear, then there is a rate of change. How can we find that?

Greg: Didn’t we have to have a ratio?

Chase: So we should look for a ratio of circumference/diameter?

Teacher: Hmmmm... that's interesting. Each group take a look at your data, and see if that tells us anything.
• For What If . . . ? Situation B, have groups share the situation they looked at, and have the other groups decide if they agree or disagree with the solutions and strategies.

Making the Mathematics Explicit

If you have collected washi tapes or string from the groups, you can begin by showing washi tapes or strings of circumference and diameters. Tape the washi tape or string lengths so they line up at the top and hang down. If you used measuring tapes, you can draw the length of the circumference and diameter on the board.

Suggested Questions

  • Look at the washi tapes or strings you cut for a circle, and compare diameter and circumference lengths. What do you notice? How are they related? (The circumference is about 3 times as long as the diameter.)
  • What is the ratio of circumference/diameter? (The ratio is a bit more than 3.)
  • If you know the diameter, can you predict the circumference? (The circumference is ≈ 3d.)
  • Does this happen with all your circles? (Yes.)
  • If you know the length of the circumference, how can you predict the length of the diameter? (Use D ≈ C/3.)
  • What patterns did you find when you compared the circumference and diameter? (For each unit of diameter, the circumference increases by the same amount, a little more than 3 units. This can be seen in the table by comparing the diameter and circumference measures.).

Some students may talk about the difference between the two amounts. If so, ask them to estimate the circumferences of circles with diameters that are not displayed, perhaps for a circle much larger than those previously measured. This relationship will not hold.

After students have verbalized the relationship between diameter and circumference, have them test the idea on a few new objects. Measure the diameter of an object, and have the class predict its circumference. Also measure the circumference of an object, and ask the class to predict the diameter.

After a few examples, push for a more exact number than “a little more than 3.” You might find the ratio of the circumference to the diameter for all the circular objects measured (which should be close to 3.1 or 3.2). Introduce the number π (pi). For these purposes, 3.14 is close enough, although you will want to tell students that this is a rounded number. For the curious student, the value of π rounded to ten decimal places is 3.1415926536.

After students have used π to find the circumferences of a few circles, have them test circles for which they have already found circumferences. Then have them work backward by finding the diameter of a circle when the circumference is given.

  • If the circumference of a circle is 100 in., what is its diameter? (about 31.8 or 32 in.)

Since this unit comes after Moving Straight Ahead, most students should be able to think about Hana’s claim in What If . . . ? Situation A. It is a nice connection back to slope, ratios, and linear relationships. Making a graph of the (diameter, circumference) class data can be helpful. This is an example:
• Is Hana’s claim correct? (Yes. It is a line with slope equal to π .)

Note that if all students use washi tapes or strings and the same measures (such as centimeters), the washi tapes or strings can be compared to see the relationship. Also, the washi tapes or strings can be used to create the graph on centimeter grid paper.

As students share the problem they worked on for What If . . . ? Situation B, encourage the class to ask questions of the other groups about the context, use of π, use of circumference, etc. Modeling some of these can start the conversation.

  • How was π important to your group in solving this problem? (Answers will vary based on the context of the problem.)
  • How was circumference a part of the context of your situation? (Answers will vary based on the context of the problem.)

Now What Do Students Know

Ask students to reflect on the discussion and answer the Now What Do You Know? questions.

See answers to the problem for more information about the strategies and embedded mathematics.

Reflecting on Student Learning  

Use the following questions to assess student understanding at the end of the lesson.  

• What evidence do I have that students understand the Now What Do You Know? Question?

  • Where did my students get stuck?
  • What strategies did they use?
  • What breakthroughs did my students have today?

• How will I use this to plan for tomorrow? For the next time I teach this lesson?

• Where will I have the opportunity to reinforce these ideas as I continue through this unit? The next unit?
